items.title: When Counties Invest in Early Childhood
items.author: Adaeze Ibeanu
items.summary: The authors evaluated the implementation of the Early Childhood Impact Fund (ECIF) in Harris County, Texas. ECIF provided $15 million to programs serving children from birth to age 5, their caregivers, and early childhood professionals.
items.body:
The authors evaluated the implementation of the Early Childhood Impact Fund (ECIF) in Harris County, Texas. ECIF represented a historic investment of more than $15 million to scale up evidence-informed programs serving children from birth to age 5, their caregivers, and early childhood professionals.

When Counties Invest in Early Childhood

Successes, Challenges, and Lessons from Harris County, Texas

Elaine Lin Wang , Karen Christianson , Jill S. Cannon , Jonathan Schweig , Adaeze Ibeanu

Research Published Sep 1, 2026

Includes Executive Summary

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Email

The Harris County Department of Economic Equity and Opportunity conceived of the Early Childhood Impact Fund (ECIF) in fall 2020. Funded primarily through the American Rescue Plan Act, ECIF represented a historic investment of more than $15 million to scale up evidence-informed programs serving children from birth to age 5, their caregivers, and early childhood professionals in Harris County, Texas. The long-term goal of ECIF, which was designed to fund six programs for two to three years each, was to strengthen outcomes for young children and families, particularly those considered vulnerable because of their income. This report presents the findings of RAND’s three-year evaluation of the implementation of ECIF.

The purposes of the evaluation were to assess progress toward initiative goals and inform future county decisionmaking. The authors formulated ten indicators to measure success across program selection, monitoring and supports for grantees, program implementation, participant satisfaction, and contributions to broader benefits for the early childhood system in Harris County. The evaluation approach included analysis of existing literature; program data; participant surveys; and interviews and focus groups with program leads, staff, and county administrators.

ECIF successfully expanded access and built some momentum for early childhood services in Harris County. The initiative demonstrated that public investment can expand early childhood supports for families and access to professional development for early childhood professionals. The initiative also highlighted system barriers—timelines, administrative complexity, and uncertain post‑grant continuation—that county leaders could address in future investments.

Key Takeaways

Collectively, grantees served far more people than initially targeted

Overall, ECIF‑funded organizations far exceeded service delivery targets. More than 30,000 children, 5,500 caregivers, and 8,500 early childhood professionals received direct benefits.

Programs reached all high‑poverty ZIP codes and primarily served Black and Hispanic families.

Many programs also provided wraparound supports and professional development for early childhood professionals.

Nearly 1.5 million meals were delivered to children and families.

Nearly 10,000 developmental screenings were provided to children.

More than 70,000 early literacy materials and resources were provided to children and families.

Participants were generally satisfied

About 90 percent of surveyed participants agreed that programs met their needs and were delivered respectfully and conveniently.

ECIF’s broader contributions were mixed

ECIF helped raise the profile of early childhood issues and efforts in the county and fostered some new partnerships.

About two‑thirds of grantees continued or expanded services after funding ended; smaller organizations faced sustainability challenges.

Program and county leads identified key lessons

Recruitment was more successful when programs actively addressed barriers to access for vulnerable families by working with community partners and providing direct support, such as transportation or translation services.

Participant feedback led to customized aspects that better addressed participant needs.

Programs needed up to one year for hiring; allotting sufficient time and resources would have helped programs scale more smoothly.

The grantee selection process should have better assessed early childhood service providers for a clear vision of goals, implementation capacity, budget assumptions, and readiness to manage public funds.

More thoughtfully structured performance indicators would have had more value for evaluating initiative success.

Recommendations

Harris County administrators should simplify oversight and reporting requirements—and provide technical assistance—to lower the burden on grantees.

Harris County administrators should plan evaluation data collection alongside program implementation to support more accurate assessment of initiative impact.

Harris County administrators should formalize and measure progress toward goals for networking and collaboration among grantees and potentially other early childhood organizations in the county.

Harris County administrators and grantees should plan for sustainability of programming and organizational capacity from day one.

Harris County administrators should invest in county-level data infrastructure to support evaluation of long-term outcomes and system-level change.

items.title: What to Watch from Trump’s US Space Academy Commission
items.author: Courtney Albon
items.summary: As President Donald Trump’s commission to study a U.S. Space Academy formulates recommendations, experts say they’ll be watching for more detail on the academy’s mission and scope as well as efforts to garner feedback from members of Congress, who will ultimately get the final say on whether the U.S. needs a space academy. The post What to Watch from Trump’s US Space Academy Commission appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine
items.body:
What to Watch from Trump’s US Space Academy Commission

Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

President Donald Trump on Aug. 28 announced plans to establish a U.S. Space Academy to bolster the country’s workforce and educate “the next generation” of space experts.

The announcement quickly drew comparisons to existing military academies—in a speech at NASA’s Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas, Trump himself likened it to the Army’s United States Military Academy at West Point. But the White House executive order issued in conjunction with the president’s announcement indicates the vision is for a new kind of federal service academy, one led by NASA and designed to train space operators and engineers across the civil, military, and commercial sectors.

“To continue to lead the world in space exploration and technology, while securing and defending our national interests in space, the Nation must prepare the next generation of astronauts, scientists, engineers, operators, entrepreneurs, civil servants, and warfighters and ensure that they are capable of advancing American interests in space,” the order states. “It is my administration’s policy to strengthen the nation’s space workforce by expanding opportunities to educate and develop the next generation of leaders across the space domain.”

The President doesn’t have the authority to create the academy on his own—that would require an act of Congress—but his order establishes a commission to explore questions around the academy’s structure, potential military or civil service requirements, location, funding, and eligibility requirements. The group will be led by NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, and other commissioners will include leaders from the White House and the Pentagon, including the Secretary of Defense and the Secretary of the Air Force. The commission is meant to issue a report with recommendations by late December.

As those recommendations take shape in the coming weeks and months, experts say they’ll be watching for more detail on the academy’s mission and scope as well as efforts to garner feedback from members of Congress. They’ll also be tracking the U.S. military’s role in the organization and how it might impact the U.S. Air Force Academy, whose 2026 class included 93 Guardians . A Department of the Air Force spokesperson declined to comment for this story. In a statement, USAFA’s Association and Foundation, its alumni organization, said it will “closely monitor developments” and share relevant information with graduates.

Charles Galbreath, director of the Mitchell Institute’s Spacepower Advantage Center of Excellence, said the concept of a NASA-led “space center of excellence” makes sense given NASA’s deep knowledge and legacy operating in the domain.

“For decades, NASA has been the repository of knowledge when it comes to space operations,” Galbreath said. “It stands to reason that it would be useful to codify that, to create an academy where NASA experts could pass on that knowledge to the next generation.”

While the President’s order doesn’t specify the primary audience for the new academy, Galbreath said there’s an opportunity to reach a wide swath of the space community—from undergraduates to mid-career operators—with programming that ranges from certifications to academic degrees. For the military, the academy could eventually serve as a means for commissioning officers, but Galbreath said that may not be necessary immediately given the Space Force’s small size.

“At some point in the future, it could grow and become a commissioning source, I suppose,” he said. “But we’re still a long way from that.”

Todd Harrison, a space policy expert at the American Enterprise Institute, said that while he agrees there’s a need to expand the space workforce, it’s not clear that a new federally run academy is the right answer. In an interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine, he cited concerns about operational costs, blurring the line between military and civil space missions, and setting up unnecessary competition with the universities that already exist to train the aerospace workforce.

Harrison suggested that rather than create a separate academy, the administration could start a scholarship program similar to the Reserve Officers’ Training Corps, or ROTC. In this scenario, the government would offer scholarships to students pursuing relevant, space-related degrees in exchange for a period of service in the Space Force, NASA, or another federal agency.

“Instead of competing with our world-class institutions . . . you would let them produce the best and the brightest talent with a commitment to go into the government and work for the government for a period of time,” he said. “Establishing a physical academy is going to take years, whereas if you make it a scholarship program, you could literally start awarding scholarships next school year.”

While a scholarship program is one way to address the government’s workforce pipeline, Galbreath argued there’s also value in creating the consolidated hub of space expertise that would come with the academy model.

“When you have people that are colocated, they’re going to breed new ideas as well,” he said. “If you’re a student and you’re learning about orbital mechanics from a NASA PhD who designed the trajectories for a multi-planetary flyby, you’re getting the best.”

Another key question for the commission is where to locate the academy. Galbreath said it’s worth considering whether the academy should be located in a single campus or dispersed across multiple hubs, adding that cost will be an important factor as the commission considers its footprint.

Harrison cautioned that opening that discussion—which is often loaded with parochial politics—too soon could muddy the process. In fact, some lawmakers have already started to pitch their districts to house the Space Academy, including Rep. Dale Strong, R-Ala., who said on Aug. 31 that Huntsville, Ala., has been floated as a potential location. Although the commission has months to recommend a location, Trump indicated he may select one sooner.

Political headwinds may become a problem for Trump’s Space Academy proposal, especially if Republicans lose their majority in either the House or Senate after midterm elections in November. Harrison said there’s likely not enough time for the commission to complete its work and put the decision to a vote before the end of this legislative session.

But Galbreath noted that creating a new academy could garner bipartisan support, similar to the creation of the Space Force in 2019 during Trump’s first term.

“It’s really going to come down to the cost-benefit—can they make a compelling case that this Space Academy is going to be worth the investment of time and money and personnel,” he said. “If they can, then I think they’ll get bipartisan support. I don’t think this is one of those areas that you can get unilateral support.”

Some Democrats, including Rep. George Whitesides, D-Calif., have already indicated they’re intrigued by the concept. In an Aug. 28 post on the social media site X, Whitesides said the idea “deserves consideration” but raised concerns about funding and the lack of congressional representation on the commission.

“I am open-minded to hear thoughtful answers to these questions, but I recommend that Congress be engaged quickly and substantively or else this intriguing idea will be stuck on the launch pad,” Whitesides said.

items.title: Lockheed Martin, General Dynamics get framework deals to surge Patriot, THAAD production
items.author: Leigh Giangreco
items.summary: The Pentagon's framework agreements with General Dynamics and Lockheed include tripling Patriot production and quadrupling THAAD interceptor output.
items.body:
MilTech

Lockheed Martin, General Dynamics get framework deals to surge Patriot, THAAD production

An attendee of a military fair in Poland looks at a PAC-3 model by Lockheed Martin. (Kacper Pempel/Reuters)

The Defense Department on Monday announced two framework agreements between General Dynamics Ordnance and Tactical Systems and Lockheed Martin to boost production of Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) and Patriot Advanced Capability-3 (PAC-3) Missile Segment Enhancement interceptors.

The agreements come as escalating conflicts with Iran and Ukraine have bled U.S. stockpiles of both THAAD and Patriot missiles.

The ongoing conflict with Iran has depleted around two-thirds of the United States’ pre-war Patriot missile interceptor inventory , according to a July report from the Center for Strategic and International Studies .

The think tank estimated that the U.S. has dispensed around 65% of its Patriot inventory and 38% of its THAAD interceptors. The U.S. is draining those supplies on two fronts, both in Iran and by transferring large stockpiles of Patriot air defense interceptors and Army Tactical Missile Systems to Ukraine.

That diminished inventory also reduces the U.S.’s ability to wage war and defend against other peer adversaries, notably China in the western Pacific, CSIS experts noted .

The U.S. recently marked six months of war with Iran, a conflict that President Donald Trump had estimated would last as little as five weeks at its outset .

With the DoD’s weapons cache dwindling, the Trump administration has turned its strategy away from military intervention and toward economic sanctions against Iran.

The framework agreements with General Dynamics and Lockheed would initiate seven-year procurement contracts to increase production quantities and accelerate delivery schedules for critical missile subcomponents, the DoD stated on Monday.

The work includes tripling Patriot production and quadrupling THAAD interceptor production capacity. However, the Pentagon also noted that the funding for that surge would be subject to annual congressional appropriations.

Earlier this month, the Pentagon announced framework agreements with Northrop Grumman and Lockheed Martin to expand Patriot and THAAD production.

items.title: US Air Force chief of staff discusses ‘regional situation’ with Israeli military officials
items.author: Cristina Stassis
items.summary: U.S. Air Force Chief of Staff Ken Wilsbach visited Israel recently and met with Israel Defense Forces and Israeli Air Force top officials.
items.body:
Mideast Africa

US Air Force chief of staff discusses ‘regional situation’ with Israeli military officials

U.S. Air Force Chief of Staff Ken Wilsbach, left, shakes hands with Israel Defense Forces Chief of the General Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir at an Aug. 23, 2026, meeting in Israel. (IDF via social media)

U.S. Air Force Chief of Staff Ken Wilsbach met with Israeli military leaders last week to discuss what Israel Defense Forces called the “regional situation” of the Iran war just before the conflict passed its six-month mark.

Wilsbach met with Israel Defense Forces Chief of the General Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir and the Commander of the Israeli Air Force Maj. Gen. Omar Tishler on Aug. 23, the IDF announced in a Wednesday social media post, with a photo of Wilsbach and Zamir shaking hands.

Wilsbach confirmed the meeting in Israel on his own social media, saying the three discussed “shared priorities for regional security” and “opportunities to deepen cooperation.”

The IDF said the groups advanced “learning from the joint campaign” as the Iran war surpassed six months.

The war, which began on Feb. 28, has consisted of dual airstrikes from both U.S. and Israeli forces, with the U.S. Air Force performing a variety of missions, including long-range bomber strikes and aerial refueling.

U.S. aircraft used in the attacks comprise a variety of bombers, strikers and refueling jets, such as the B-1B Lancer, B-52 Stratofortress, F-15E Strike Eagle, KC-135 Stratotanker, F-35A Lightning II and A-10 Thunderbolt II.

Wilsbach’s recent visit to Israel is the first publicly announced meeting, even though the chief of staff previously visited seven U.S. bases across the Middle East and Europe within the U.S. Central Command and U.S. European Command’s area of responsibility in December 2025.

Since the war began, 18 U.S. service members have died . The Pentagon has since altered the way it classifies casualties suffered, moving four to another casualty summary and thus lowering the number to 14.

Cristina Stassis is a reporter covering stories surrounding the defense industry, national security, military/veteran affairs and more. She previously worked as an editorial fellow for Defense News in 2024 where she assisted the newsroom in breaking news across Sightline Media Group.

items.title: Not All ‘Magic’ Mushrooms Are the Same
items.summary: Millions of U.S. adults use Amanita muscaria mushrooms. But these distinctive fungi aren’t like other psychoactive mushrooms. What do consumers and policymakers need to know about them?
items.body:
Not All ‘Magic’ Mushrooms Are the Same

Commentary

Aug 31, 2026

Photo by Robin Verhoef/Getty Images

By Michelle Priest and Beau Kilmer

This commentary was originally published by San Francisco Chronicle on August 29, 2026.

Mushrooms are everywhere in California—literally and figuratively. Some are edible, some are psychoactive, some are toxic. And in the case of Amanita muscaria mushrooms, they can be all three.

You may not yet have heard of Amanita muscaria , also called “fly agaric,” but you certainly have seen images of it. The orange-, yellow- or red-capped mushroom with white spots is in everything from “Alice in Wonderland” to Super Mario video games. In our recent RAND report on the use of psychedelics , we estimated that about 3.5 million American adults used Amanita muscaria in 2025, compared with 11 million who reported using psychoactive psilocybin mushrooms.

Psilocybin mushrooms and Amanita muscaria are not the same. Given the growing popularity of so-called “magic” mushrooms for recreational and therapeutic use, as well as possible confusion between these different mushrooms, policymakers and health officials should not ignore health concerns related to Amanita muscaria .

This is especially true because of the media attention psilocybin has received. Emerging clinical research has shown promise in using psilocybin for treating a variety of mental health ailments. Yet despite growing public interest, psilocybin has not been approved as a medicine by the Food and Drug Administration and remains illegal under federal law. Federal prohibition has not stopped some states and localities from moving ahead. In addition to three states legalizing supervised psilocybin use, more than 30 cities and counties have “deprioritized” the enforcement of certain offenses related to psychedelics, including psilocybin.

About 3.5 million American adults used Amanita muscaria in 2025, compared with 11 million who reported using psychoactive psilocybin mushrooms.

Oakland was an early mover in this space. In 2019, the City Council passed a resolution making the investigation and arrest of adults “for planting, cultivating, purchasing, transporting, distributing, engaging in practices with, and/or possessing” psilocybin mushrooms and other naturally occurring psychedelics one of the lowest priorities for local law enforcement.

But not all psychedelic mushrooms are the same.

Unlike the vast majority ( PDF ) of mushrooms containing psilocybin, Amanita muscaria can be quite toxic . If not properly prepared, effects can include nausea and vomiting, with more severe cases involving seizures, coma and, in extremely rare instances, death .

Most people who use Amanita muscaria do not run into problems, but a recent international review highlighted some troubling anecdotes. In one case report , an older couple was rushed to the hospital after consuming Amanita muscaria . They both went into severe comas, and one had a seizure, in addition to other serious symptoms. Thankfully, after intensive medical treatment, each made a full recovery.

The main active compound in Amanita muscaria is muscimol, which acts primarily on neurotransmitters in the brain. The most common self-reported effects are an intoxicated feeling similar to alcohol, sleepiness (sometimes with altered dreams), and relaxation. Others report that it can help reduce substance use or alleviate anxiety, but no clinical trials have confirmed these health claims .

The mushroom is not hard to find.

Amanita muscaria grows in many parts of the country. The California State Parks Foundation website even features a picture of it growing in Salt Point State Park in Sonoma County. It is also sold in unregulated gummies, chocolates, and other products.

And, yes, people report using it to microdose, too.

Amanita muscaria is not illegal under the federal Controlled Substances Act. And only one state, Louisiana, prohibits it. A 2024 assessment by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration ( PDF ) found that it is not safe to eat or add to food, but minimal action has been taken to get these products out of brick-and-mortar and online shops.

Given its risk profile and legal status, there are concerns about unregulated products advertising with images of Amanita muscaria or claims that they contain it. These products may contain Amanita muscaria , or they may not. They may also contain a mix of other unregulated intoxicants that can be harmful. A 2026 review from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention identified 180 cases of severe illness in 34 states associated with eating mushroom-containing products, including some that contained compounds from Amanita muscaria and psilocybin mushrooms along with other substances. The California Department of Public Health has also raised concerns about the substances that are in widely available mushroom products.

The popularity and accessibility of Amanita muscaria suggests public health agencies should step up education campaigns that highlight their specific risks.

State and federal policymakers have many options when it comes to Amanita muscaria and products claiming to contain it, and each has unique costs and benefits .

For example, prohibition is an option, although enforcing the law against those foraging for mushrooms would be difficult. Jurisdictions could also allow adults to grow and possess Amanita muscaria but prohibit retail sales, as Colorado has done with psilocybin mushrooms and some other nature-based psychedelics. If states decide to regulate production and sales, they’ll confront many decisions around child-proof packaging requirements, product testing, marketing restrictions, taxes, and how these products can be sold.

Regardless of any legal or regulatory changes, the popularity and accessibility of Amanita muscaria suggests public health agencies should step up education campaigns that highlight their specific risks .

Not all mind-altering mushrooms are the same. In the current environment, consumers need to know that what they are buying is unregulated and may contain other harmful products.

Although Amanita muscaria isn’t as popular as psilocybin, it’s time for policy and public health conversations to include the other magic mushroom.

items.title: Mirror Life Is Theoretical. The Danger Is Anything But.
items.summary: With mirror life, scientists have given world leaders both the foresight and the time to address the danger. What's needed isn't alarm but action to ensure that mirror life remains just a footnote in human history—and not its final chapter.
items.body:
Mirror Life Is Theoretical. The Danger Is Anything But.

Commentary

Aug 31, 2026

Image by Ake Puttisarn/Getty Images

By Nidhi Kalra

This commentary was originally published by the Washington Post on August 31, 2026.

“This includes creation of mirror organisms.” These six bland words appear as a footnote in the White House policy for “Stopping High-Risk Life Sciences Research” ( PDF ) released in July—but they shouldn't be treated like one.

If you've never heard of mirror life—the more commonly used term for mirror organisms—there's a good reason: It doesn't exist. But this sci-fi-sounding form of life could theoretically be built out of biological molecules that are mirror images of the ones that exist naturally.

The idea emerges from the fact that nearly all biomolecules in nature have a kind of handedness—all DNA, for example, is built from right-handed sugars, and all proteins are made from left-handed amino acids. Thus, it's possible to imagine—and maybe even create—a living organism made of mirror-image counterparts to natural biomolecules. The first would probably be mirror bacteria.

That may not sound like reason for alarm. But scientists warn that mirror bacteria could devastate most life on earth. In 2024, dozens of them issued an urgent call to prevent mirror bacteria from ever being created, saying, “We cannot rule out a scenario in which a mirror bacterium acts as an invasive species across many ecosystems, causing pervasive lethal infections in a substantial fraction of plant and animal species, including humans.”

Yet we are edging closer to the threshold of mirror life. Over the past decade, biologists have engineered specialized tools for replicating and assembling mirror-image biomolecules. These tools could have some uses: For example, medicines made from mirror biomolecules could evade the processes that normally break them down, so treatments based on them might be longer-lasting than treatments based on regular biomolecules.

Certain advances could also become stepping stones toward mirror bacteria, and that's where the danger lurks.

But certain advances could also become stepping stones toward mirror bacteria, and that's where the danger lurks. Mirror bacteria might not be recognized by the things—immune systems, enzymes and other predator microorganisms—that keep normal bacteria in check. Outside of a lab, it might spread out of control, which is why no one should ever create it.

The good news is that the breakthroughs required to make mirror life are probably 10 to 30 years away , and very few scientists are even equipped to make the attempt. If the world's leading scientists desist, they will effectively deny the means to everyone else.

So here's the call to action: As Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping meet in September to explore areas of cooperation, they should put prevention of mirror life on the agenda. If the two leaders seek a topic of global importance they can agree on, surely this is it. Mirror life is a shared existential risk with no credible upside for either country.

Instead, they can lay a foundation for universal restraint. A first step would be for the two countries to articulate a shared belief that there should be boundaries between acceptable and unacceptable research in this field. They could produce joint ethical standards for researchers, plus issue public statements that make it clear that mirror life is not a legitimate area of scientific pursuit.

Deciding exactly where to draw boundaries regarding mirror life research should involve collaborative discussions. The goals should be to determine when potentially beneficial early research steps onto a slippery slope.

As Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping meet in September to explore areas of cooperation, they should put prevention of mirror life on the agenda.

For instance, some scientists have suggested that the mirror version of a ribosome—the machinery in cells that makes proteins—could make it easier to produce mirror proteins for medical use. But a mirror ribosome would also be a huge step toward creating mirror life. Instead, the United States and China might agree to prohibit the development of mirror ribosomes and work together on other ways to make mirror proteins.

This should lead to formal agreements not to pursue mirror life, along with jointly establishing economic and logistical barriers to its creation.

Some will dismiss hopes of such cooperation between strategic competitors as gross naiveté. But history has shown that cooperation among rivals is possible when the stakes are high enough.

In 1967, in the depths of Cold War animosity, the U.S. and Soviet Union together championed the Intensified Smallpox Eradication Program. With joint leadership—money, logistics and more than a billion Soviet vaccine doses—smallpox was successfully eradicated worldwide in 1980. Beijing and Washington can take inspiration from this example to protect the entire biosphere.

It's rare to meet a moment when the risks of a scientific breakthrough are so clear. More typically, it's too early to tell or too late to fix. With mirror life, scientists have given world leaders both the foresight and the time to address the danger. What's needed isn't alarm but action to ensure that mirror life remains just a footnote in human history—and not its final chapter.

items.title: Preparing Students for What Comes Next
items.author: Elizabeth D. Steiner
items.summary: The authors analyze data from three RAND survey panels to examine career-connected learning in kindergarten through grade 12 schools in academic year 2025–2026 using the perspectives of district leaders, school leaders, and high school students.
items.body:
The authors analyze data from three RAND survey panels to examine career-connected learning in kindergarten through grade 12 schools in academic year 2025–2026. They explore this topic using the perspectives of district leaders, school leaders, and school students. This report can inform policymakers and education leaders across the United States who are working to design or strengthen career-connected learning opportunities for students.

Preparing Students for What Comes Next

Educator and Student Perspectives on Career-Connected Learning in K–12 Schools

Benjamin K. Master , Melissa Kay Diliberti , Cristina Alvarez , AK Keskin , Elizabeth D. Steiner

Research Published Aug 31, 2026

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Email

Increasingly, when employers hire entry-level workers, they are placing a higher value on candidates who have a variety of skills and experiences. As the labor market for young adults shifts accordingly, educators are facing a growing need to understand how kindergarten through grade 12 (K–12) students learn about and navigate college and career pathways. Research on how schools help students explore career fields and gain professional experience is therefore a key complement to research on traditional college preparation supports.

In academic year 2025–2026, the authors of this report gathered survey data from district leaders via the American School District Panel, from school principals via the American School Leader Panel, and from students via the American Youth Panel. These data included information about college advisory and preparatory activities and work-related learning. Together, the three survey panels offer a timely and nationally representative view of career-connected programming in K–12 public schools and students’ experiences with that programming. These findings can inform policymakers, workforce development coordinators, career and technical education directors, and school leaders across the United States who are seeking to design or strengthen these learning opportunities.

Key Takeaways

Career-connected learning in high school centers on pathways to college. Sixty-six percent of high school students reported hearing a lot of emphasis from educators about attending a four-year college, while other pathways received much less emphasis.

Most leaders described providing students with their first experiences with career-connected learning in middle school, with most districts offering some form of career exploration or planning support.

Students described making after high school plans late in their high school careers: By spring of their junior year, more than four in ten students had yet to make a plan or meet with their counselors about college and career plans.

Students’ plans for work-related learning consistently outpace their follow-through. By spring of their senior year, only 39 percent reported visiting an employer or workplace, even though 71 percent said that they had planned to do so; only 22 percent had actually participated in an internship or apprenticeship, even though 66 percent indicated that they had planned to do so.

Sixty-three percent of high schools set numeric targets for students to meet with guidance counselors about college or a career, and around half of high schools (52 percent) set targets related to students developing postsecondary plans. Few track whether students are accepted to college or secure employment after high school.

Students who do not want to pursue a bachelor’s degree rated their schools’ supports the most negatively. Students from lower-income families were also less likely to report that school supports are well-matched to their families’ financial situations.

items.title: The 988 Lifeline’s Integration Into the Broader Crisis Care Continuum
items.author: Ryan K. McBain
items.summary: The objective of this paper is to understand how 988 Lifeline centers are connected to the broader crisis care continuum, including 911, mobile crisis response, and community-based services.
items.body:
The 988 Lifeline’s Integration Into the Broader Crisis Care Continuum

Stephanie Brooks Holliday , Samantha Matthews , Rachel Slover , James Liu , Joshua Breslau , Jonathan Purtle , Vikram Kilambi , Megan S. Schuler , Rajeev Ramchand , Beth Ann Griffin , et al.

Research Posted on rand.org Aug 31, 2026 Published in: AJPM Focus (2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.focus.2026.100551

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Email

Objective

To understand how 988 Lifeline centers are connected to the broader crisis care continuum—including 911, mobile crisis response, and community-based services.

Methods

The authors conducted a cross-sectional survey of 988 Lifeline centers in the U.S. between May and July 2025. A total of 159 centers (78%) completed the survey, which assessed transfer to/from 911, coordination with mobile crisis teams, capacity for referrals, and tracking dispositions and outcomes. Exploratory bivariate analyses were conducted to understand the factors associated with transfers to/from 911 and mobile crisis response team dispatch capability.

Results

Approximately 45% of centers reported bidirectional interoperability with 911. Among the 153 centers with a mobile crisis response team in their service region, 61% could dispatch the team directly. Exploratory bivariate analysis indicated that centers had higher odds of interoperating with 911 when mobile crisis services were present throughout their jurisdiction (OR = 2.10 [1.06, 4.20]) and could schedule appointments on callers’ behalf (OR = 2.88 [1.39, 6.23]).

Conclusions

Variation remains in centers’ ability to interoperate with 911 and dispatch mobile crisis teams. Centers with these capabilities were associated with having multiple referral, dispatch, and coordination capacities. Improving integration between 988 and other crisis services requires strengthened partnerships, sustainable funding, and investments in technology and data-sharing infrastructure.

items.title: From Support to Priority
items.author: AK Keskin
items.summary: This is the second brief in CRPE and RAND’s three-part series on the state of civic learning in U.S. school districts.
items.body:
From Support to Priority

How Formal Structures Can Help Districts Protect Time for Civics Learning

Lisa Chu , AK Keskin

Research Posted on rand.org Aug 31, 2026 Published in: Center on Reinventing Public Education website (August 2026)

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Email

Civic learning is having a moment. But what actually makes it stick as a priority in schools? New national survey data from the American School District Panel (ASDP)—a research partnership between CRPE and RAND—find signs of growing momentum: 20% of district leaders said their district had increased its prioritization of civic learning over the past year, while 18% reported increased school board support. But interviews with district leaders reveal an important wrinkle: support was strongest when civic learning was grounded in local engagement, and weaker when it was perceived as politically charged or connected to national debates. And support alone isn’t enough. Leaders who described civics as a clear district priority, woven into learning goals and other existing structures, had an easier time protecting a commitment to civic learning.

items.title: From Occurrence to Consequence
items.author: Thomas Gernay
items.summary: In this work, we analyze more than one million fire incident reports and integrate them with community-level socioeconomic indicators, building inventories, weather conditions, and incident-specific characteristics.
items.body:
Building fires remain a major public safety concern in U.S. cities, threatening lives, property, and critical infrastructure. Despite substantial investments in fire protection, significant disparities persist, underscoring the need for a holistic, data-driven understanding of fire risk. In this work, we analyze more than one million fire incident reports and integrate them with community-level socioeconomic indicators, building inventories, weather conditions, and incident-specific characteristics. Our study makes two key contributions: a comprehensive framework that traces fire risk from occurrence to consequence, and a detailed city-level fire risk ranking system for U.S. cities. By examining the full progression of fire events, we identify structural, environmental, and social drivers that disproportionately endanger communities with older infrastructure and economic disadvantages. Socioeconomic disparities intensify both the frequency and severity of fire incidents, while incident-specific factors, such as ignition sources, ignition locations, and the presence of detectors or automatic extinguishing systems, substantially influence fire outcomes. Lower-risk cities generally exhibit more favorable socioeconomic conditions and a higher prevalence of fire safety features. By pinpointing high-risk communities and targeting critical vulnerabilities, this framework supports strategies that further improve fire safety and foster more resilient cities.

An Important Domain for Applied Science

This Special Feature on illegal markets gathers, perhaps for the first time, papers by some of the world’s leading experts on nine different illegal markets. All are tasked with describing “their” market via a common analytic lens that focuses on the markets’ structure and how they operate. Two additional papers synthesize the main findings from these articles, focusing on analytic commonalities and implications for policy. Collectively, these 11 papers raise questions that may motivate other researchers to work on these topics, possibly spurring conversations about whether illegal markets should become a more prominent field of scientific inquiry.

items.title: Feasibility and Acceptability of a Compassion-Focused Program to Support Staff, Improve Workflows and Enhance the Clinic Environment in South African Primary Health Clinics with Low ART Retention
items.author: Virginia Zweigenthal
items.summary: We used a positive deviance (PD) approach to develop a program called Connect designed to increase retention in HIV care by improving the staff and patient experience in South Africa.
items.body:
South Africa has the largest HIV epidemic globally. Despite improvement, retention on antiretroviral therapy (ART) remains challenging. We used a positive deviance (PD) approach to develop a program called Connect designed to increase retention in HIV care by improving the staff and patient experience. PD consists of discovering ways in which high-performing outliers succeed despite sizable barriers and then sharing successful strategies with lower performers. Connect consists of strategies in three domains: (1) engaging, encouraging, supporting staff; (2) expediting and augmenting workflow; (3) creating a welcoming environment. In a pilot study to determine feasibility and acceptability, we conducted interviews or focus groups with leadership (N = 8) and staff (N = 12) and administered acceptability surveys (N = 20) and compassion training satisfaction surveys (N = 67) in three public health clinics in Cape Town. We reviewed implementation logs to assess feasibility and analyzed surveys and qualitative perspectives to determine acceptability. Huddles and compassion training was highly acceptable, but attendance in huddles was low, and they were not delivered as intended. Aesthetic improvements were not feasible, and workflow improvements were already implemented. A larger study is needed to test the effectiveness of huddles and compassion training on ART retention.

items.title: Patient and Caregiver Perspectives on Communication Quality in Tele-Palliative Care
items.author: Jordan M. Harrison
items.summary: This paper qualitatively explores patient and family caregiver experiences with telehealth and in-person visits for outpatient palliative care, including preferences related to mode of care and any perceived differences in communication quality by mode in a post-pandemic context.
items.body:
Patient and Caregiver Perspectives on Communication Quality in Tele-Palliative Care

Julia Bandini , Elaine Li , Dio Kavalieratos , Natalie C. Ernecoff , Kimberly A. Curseen , Jordan M. Harrison

Research Posted on rand.org Aug 31, 2026 Published in: Journal of Palliative Medicine (2026). DOI: 10.1177/10966218261484819

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Email

Background

Tele-palliative care has become a well-established practice following its rapid expansion in the outpatient setting during the COVID-19 pandemic. Despite sustained integration of tele-palliative care, questions remain about patients’ and family caregivers’ experiences with it and its potential impact on the quality of communication during palliative care visits. Objective: To qualitatively explore patient and family caregiver experiences with telehealth and in-person visits for outpatient palliative care, including preferences related to mode of care and any perceived differences in communication quality by mode in a post-pandemic context.

Methods

We conducted semistructured interviews with 26 participants (15 patients and 11 family caregivers) receiving outpatient palliative care at one academic medical center in the southern United States.

Results

Three themes emerged: (1) participants weighed convenience, symptom burden, and visit reason in choosing mode of care; (2) opinions differed on the authenticity of communication via telehealth; and (3) comfort and privacy shaped communication quality. Some patients and family caregivers perceived communication via telehealth as comparable to in-person care, while others felt in-person visits allowed for more authentic interactions. Many found that the convenience of telehealth outweighed any perceived differences in communication quality. In addition, some patients noted that without the option for telehealth, the benefits of an in-person palliative care visit may not have outweighed the travel burden.

Conclusions

Telehealth can support high-quality communication and offer meaningful access for outpatient palliative care. A hybrid model of care provides a person-centered approach to meet the needs of patients with serious illness and their family caregivers.

items.title: Mental Health Care Use and Barriers Among Veterans and Nonveterans With Suicidal Ideation
items.author: Rajeev Ramchand
items.summary: The authors estimated the prevalence rates of mental health service use in a national sample of veterans with recent suicidal ideation, compared rates with those of nonveterans, and identified barriers to care.
items.body:
Mental Health Care Use and Barriers Among Veterans and Nonveterans With Suicidal Ideation

Findings From a National Survey

Julia Lejeune , Carrie M. Farmer , Rajeev Ramchand

Research Posted on rand.org Aug 31, 2026 Published in: Psychiatric Services (2026). DOI: 10.1176/appi.ps.20250415

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Email

Objective

Since 2001, suicide rates among veterans have exceeded and risen faster than those of nonveterans. Although policy efforts have expanded suicide prevention and mental health services in the Veterans Health Administration (VHA), limited data exist on service use and barriers among veterans at high risk for suicide, especially those outside VHA care. The authors estimated the prevalence rates of mental health service use in a national sample of veterans with recent suicidal ideation, compared rates with those of nonveterans, and identified barriers to care.

Methods

Data were drawn from pooled 2015–2019 National Survey on Drug Use and Health assessments (N=214,395 adults, including 11,875 veterans). Survey-weighted Poisson regression analyses adjusted for demographic covariates were used to compare mental health service use, unmet treatment needs, and treatment barriers between veterans and nonveterans with recent suicidal ideation.

Results

Among adults with suicidal ideation, veterans more commonly used mental health services than did nonveterans (56.0% vs. 47.3%) and had a higher likelihood of past-year outpatient treatment (adjusted prevalence ratio [APR]=1.26) and pharmacological treatment (APR=1.17). However, nearly one-third of both veterans and nonveterans reported unmet mental health needs. Veterans were less likely than nonveterans to endorse cost as a barrier to care (APR=0.65) but were more likely to endorse confidentiality concerns (APR=1.65). Fear of involuntary hospitalization and stigma were common in both groups.

Conclusions

Despite higher service use and fewer cost-related barriers, veterans with suicidal ideation still reported high unmet needs, underscoring the importance of addressing persistent barriers and improving care quality for veterans at elevated suicide risk.

items.author: Eunice C. Wong
items.summary: Given the role of religion in U.S. Latino communities and their elevated risk for PTSD, this study examined associations among PTSD, religious involvement, and marital functioning, and whether religious involvement moderated the associations.
items.body:
The U.S. Latino community faces elevated risks for marital distress given stressors such as economic hardship and immigration-related challenges, but there has been limited research on protective and risk factors associated with marital outcomes among this population. Given the prominent role of religion in U.S. Latino communities and their elevated risk for posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), this study examined associations among PTSD, religious involvement, and marital functioning, as well as whether religious involvement moderated the association between PTSD and marital functioning. This study used secondary data from 1,288 married Latino individuals in the National Latino and Asian American Study. Multiple linear regression analyses examined associations between religious involvement (religious service attendance and coping), lifetime PTSD diagnosis, and marital functioning (cohesion and conflict). Higher religious service attendance was linked to higher marital cohesion and lower marital conflict, whereas seeking comfort in religion during difficult times was associated with higher marital conflict. Lifetime PTSD was associated with higher marital conflict, and this association was not significantly moderated by religious involvement. These findings are valuable for understanding the factors associated with marital functioning among Latino couples and suggest that religious service attendance may be a relational resource, whereas certain types of coping may be associated with greater marital conflict. Considering the religiocultural context may inform interventions and support services that leverage resources and values embedded within religious communities to promote marital functioning among Latino couples.

items.title: Patterns of Institutional Trust During COVID-19
items.author: Lynsay Ayer
items.summary: To explore patterns of institutional trust among adults in the United States Gulf Coast region, we utilized data from the Survey of Trauma, Resilience, and Opportunity among Neighborhoods in the Gulf.
items.body:
Institutional trust significantly affects compliance with public health measures, such as those implemented during the coronavirus disease 2019 pandemic, including social distancing, mask-wearing, and vaccination. To explore patterns of institutional trust among adults in the United States Gulf Coast region, we utilized data from the Survey of Trauma, Resilience, and Opportunity among Neighborhoods in the Gulf. This survey evaluated trust levels across six institutions: local, state, and federal governments, local religious organizations, academia, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Employing latent class analysis, we identified three trust patterns: high, medium, and low. Regression analysis revealed demographic differences between the classes, indicating that Black or Hispanic individuals are less likely to be in the low-trust group, whereas those identifying as more religious are more likely to belong to the low-trust group compared to the medium- or high-trust groups. These findings suggest that in future pandemics and emergencies, officials and policymakers should collaborate with local religious leaders to ensure that all community members receive crucial information from trusted sources. This approach may enhance compliance with public health directives.

items.body:
WRIGHT-PATTERSON AIR FORCE BASE, Ohio -- In a show of artificial intelligence in space, the Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) recently demonstrated autonomous control of a satellite bus using a neural network. The flight marks a pivotal shift from AI managing sensors and payloads to it directly commanding the critical function of spacecraft orientation.

During the mission, an AI agent was uplinked to a CubeSat orbiting hundreds of miles above Earth. Within a single orbit and without human intervention, the neural network autonomously controlled the spacecraft's orientation, precisely steering the vehicle to its mission objective and avoiding hazardous conditions

"We have a responsibility to translate advances in AI to give our Airmen and Guardians trustworthy autonomous teammates to meet today's fast-moving challenges,” said Department of the Air Force Technology Executive Officer and AFRL Commander Brig. Gen. Douglas P. Wickert . “The AFRL vision is to win the future by executing our mission to discover, develop and deliver war-winning science and technology." ~ Brig. Gen. Douglas P. Wickert, Air Force Technology Executive Officer and AFRL Commander

"We have a responsibility to translate advances in AI to give our Airmen and Guardians trustworthy autonomous teammates to meet today's fast-moving challenges,” said Department of the Air Force Technology Executive Officer and AFRL Commander Brig. Gen. Douglas P. Wickert . “The AFRL vision is to win the future by executing our mission to discover, develop and deliver war-winning science and technology."

~ Brig. Gen. Douglas P. Wickert, Air Force Technology Executive Officer and AFRL Commander

AFRL's Autonomy Capability Team (ACT3) trained the neural network using reinforcement learning and subjected it to extensive pre-flight simulation and laboratory testing, bridging the gap between simulated environments and physical operations ahead of uploading it to the test vehicle.

“We used startup-like agility to take a reinforcement learning model from the lab directly to orbit,” said Dr. Steve “Cap” Rogers , AFRL senior scientist for AI enabled autonomy. “This flight is a perfect example of ACT3's core mission to operationalize AI at scale for the Air and Space Force.”

To ensure mission safety, the flight also tested a next-generation AI watchdog system and AFRL-designed guardrail runtime assurance systems. Watchdogs detect when AI systems approach unverified situations, enabling them to pivot seamlessly to backup systems. Guardrails monitor vehicle state and neural network outputs, intervening when predefined safety boundaries are approached. These systems ran in “shadow mode” and provided insight to how each would respond to the neural network in real time.

With the foundational capabilities of neural network control now proven in orbit, AFRL plans to expand the scope and complexity of autonomous operations for future flights.

About AFRL The Air Force Research Laboratory is the Department of the Air Force’s primary scientific research and development center and one of six centers within Air Force Materiel Command. AFRL leads the discovery, development and delivery of technologies for air, space and the multidomain. With a workforce spanning seven mission areas at more than 40 locations worldwide, AFRL conducts research ranging from basic science to advanced technology development. For more information, visit: afresearchlab.com .

About ACT3 AFRL’s ACT3 is an AI Special Operations organization whose mission is to Operationalize AI at Scale for the Air Force and the Space Force. Commissioned by the AFRL Commander, ACT3 leverages an innovative ‘start-up’ business model as an alternative approach to the traditional AFRL Technical Directorate R&D model by combining the blue sky vision of an academic institution; the flexibility of an AI startup; and the discipline of a production development company. The goal of the ACT3 business model is to define the shortest path to successful transition of solutions using AFRL’s internal expertise and collaborations with the best academic and commercial AI researchers in the world. Successful implementation may mean new technology or new implementation of existing technology. To learn more about ACT3, visit: afrl.af.mil/ACT3/
